steps.prompt: How does a robot learn to move with nobody showing it the moves?
steps.sub: No one writes the perfect walk. The robot tries, gets a score, adjusts, and tries again — thousands of times. That's reinforcement learning. By the end you'll name its four parts and trace a robot earning its first reward.

steps.prompt: First instinct — a robot is learning to stand up. How does RL actually teach it?

options.t: An engineer types the exact angle for every joint at every instant.
The robot tries random-ish moves, gets a higher score when it stays upright longer, and shifts toward whatever earned more score.
The robot copies a video of a human standing up, frame by frame.

steps.why: Reinforcement learning is trial-and-error with a score. The robot acts, the world hands back a reward (higher for staying up), and it nudges its behavior toward whatever earned more. No human dictates the joint angles, and it's not copying a video — it discovers the skill by chasing reward.
hints: The word is 'reinforcement' — something gets reinforced when it works.
Nobody hand-types the moves. What signal tells the robot a try went well?

steps.prompt: The four parts of every RL setup — framed for movement.
steps.sub: Tap each card. Memorize these four; the whole field is built on them.

cards.b: The decider — the policy in the robot's 'brain' that picks the next action: how much torque to send each joint.
The simulated world + the robot's body. It takes the action and returns the new state plus a reward.
A number scoring how good that move was. Higher for moving toward the goal, lower for falling.
One full attempt — start, act, act, act, until it succeeds, falls, or time runs out. Then reset and try again.

steps.prompt: A robot arm is learning to reach a target. Sort each piece into the right RL part.
steps.sub: Tap an item, then tap the part it belongs to.

items.t: The policy deciding how to swing the arm next
The simulated table, target, and arm's physics
+1 when the hand gets closer to the target
One attempt: start → reach → reset, capped at 5 seconds

hints: The AGENT decides; the ENVIRONMENT reacts and scores.
The REWARD is the number; the EPISODE is one whole try from start to reset.

steps.prompt: In RL, which part DECIDES the action, and which part JUDGES it?
steps.sub: Two halves of every RL loop. Don't mix them up.

options.t: The environment decides the action; the agent judges it.
The agent decides the action; the environment returns the new state and the reward.
The reward decides the action; the episode judges it.

steps.why: The agent (the policy) is the decider — it chooses the action. The environment is the judge and the world — it applies the action, evolves the physics, and hands back the new state plus a reward. Reward and episode are pieces the environment produces, not deciders.
hints: Which part has the 'brain' that picks a move? That's the decider.
Which part is the world that reacts and hands back a score? That's the judge.

steps.prompt: Tap the steps of one turn of the RL loop in order — then it repeats.
steps.sub: This little cycle runs over and over within every episode.
chips: Environment returns the new state + a reward
Agent updates itself to earn more reward next time
hints: It has to SEE the situation before it can choose a move.
Observe → act → get the score → learn from it, then loop.

steps.prompt: Watch a real run. Walk a hopping robot through its first few RL turns.
steps.sub: At each turn, pick the move that fits how RL learns. The log fills in as you go.
steps.goal: Learn to hop forward without falling. Reward = +1 per cm moved forward, big penalty for falling.

turns.situation: Episode 1 begins. The robot stands at the start, knowing nothing about hopping.
turns.q: What does the agent do on its very first move?
options: Try a roughly-random action and see what reward comes back
Refuse to move until an engineer types the perfect hop
Copy a YouTube video of a kangaroo
turns.log: 🧠 Agent → tries a random-ish leg push.

turns.situation: The push made it lurch forward 3 cm, then it wobbled but stayed up.
turns.q: The environment now responds. What does it hand back?
options: A new state (robot tilted, moved 3 cm) plus reward +3
The exact correct next action to take

turns.situation: It got +3 for that push. A different jerky move earlier had given it -10 (a fall).
turns.q: What does the agent do with these two results?
options: Shift toward moves like the +3 one, away from the -10 one
Ignore the rewards and keep acting randomly forever
Quit, because one move already worked
turns.log: 📈 Agent updates → favor +3 push, avoid the fall.

turns.situation: This attempt ends — it fell after 8 cm. Time and progress logged.
turns.q: One try is over. What happens next in RL?
options: Reset to the start and run another episode, a bit smarter
Stop forever — RL trains on a single attempt
Keep the robot frozen where it fell

hints: RL learns by trying, scoring, and adjusting — over MANY episodes.
Higher reward = do more of that. Lower reward = do less of that.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: In RL, an engineer hand-writes the correct action for every situation.
statements.why: No — that's the whole point of RL. The robot discovers good actions by trial-and-error guided by reward, instead of being told each move.

statements.t: An episode is one full attempt, after which the robot resets and tries again.
statements.why: Right — an episode runs from start until success, failure, or time-out, then resets. Learning happens across thousands of episodes.

statements.t: Reward is feedback the environment gives back, not a command the agent sends out.
statements.why: Correct — the agent sends an action; the environment sends back the new state and a reward number. Reward flows toward the agent.

statements.t: The agent and the environment are just two names for the same thing.
statements.why: No — they're two halves. The agent is the decider (the policy); the environment is the world that reacts and scores. Keeping them separate is key to understanding RL.

hints: Recall the loop: observe → act → get reward → update.
Who decides, and who judges? Those are two different parts.
